trystero is a header-only port of Trystero 0.26.0’s serverless WebRTC rooms for C++20, one of the libraries of webcpp. Peers find each other over public Nostr relays and exchange messages directly, over WebRTC data channels. The wire is Trystero’s: a room joined from C++ and the same room joined from Trystero’s JavaScript are one room.

This page teaches trystero section by section: what a room is, how a program joins one in the browser and natively, how its actions carry messages, where its memory comes from, what each backend asks of its platform, the wire it speaks, and what it guarantees. Every program it shows is one of the library’s examples, which the build compiles and links on its target. None is run by the build, since each needs the public relays or a browser, so the page shows no output of theirs. The reference lists every name the headers declare.

Overview

trystero lets programs meet in a room and exchange messages directly, peer to peer, over WebRTC data channels. There is no server of the application’s own: peers find each other by publishing short signed messages on public Nostr relays, exchange the WebRTC offer and answer through them, and from then on talk over the connection the browser or the network stack established.

It ports the protocol of Trystero 0.26.0, and keeps its wire byte for byte. A room joined from C++ and the same room joined from Trystero’s JavaScript are one room: the peers see each other, and an action sent from one side arrives on the other.

The library provides:

  • room, which joins a room of an application over Nostr relays, reports the peers that join and leave, measures round trips, and leaves with Trystero’s farewell;

  • action<T>, a named channel of messages: text, JSON (boost::json::value), binary, or any of the three, with optional JSON metadata, of any size, sent inline or in chunks with backpressure;

  • the password of a room, part of the key that seals the signaling and a challenge added to the handshake;

  • every asynchronous operation as an Asio initiating function, so it completes with a callback, boost::asio::use_awaitable, boost::asio::deferred or any other completion token;

  • a memory resource per room, which every allocation of the room goes through (Allocation);

  • a backend interface that separates the room from the platform, and its two implementations, for the browser and for native programs.

Two backends

<webcpp/trystero.hpp> is the rooms themselves, which build on both of trystero’s targets, native and emscripten, and include neither backend. Each backend is a header of its own:

Backend Target Built on

<webcpp/trystero/browser/backend.hpp>

emscripten

the page’s WebSocket, RTCPeerConnection, RTCDataChannel, setTimeout and crypto.subtle, through embind (The browser backend)

<webcpp/trystero/native/backend.hpp>

native

libdatachannel for WebRTC, Boost.Beast for the relays’ WebSockets, OpenSSL for TLS and AES-GCM, and Asio’s timers (The native backend)

Both run the same room, and both meet Trystero JS peers. Every name is in the namespace webcpp::trystero.

Requirements

  • A C++20 compiler.

  • Boost 1.92: Asio, Container (its pmr base class), Core, Hash2, JSON and System; and Beast for the native backend.

  • libsecp256k1 0.8.0, with its schnorrsig and extrakeys modules, for the BIP-340 signatures of Nostr events: every room needs it.

  • In the browser: Emscripten 6.0.11, the version webcpp pins, and a page served from a secure context (https, or http on localhost), where crypto.subtle exists.

  • Natively: libdatachannel 0.24.6 and OpenSSL 3, and exceptions (Exceptions).

trystero raises no exception of its own: an operation that can fail completes with an error code. The rooms, the protocol and the browser backend compile without exceptions; so do the native timer, sealer and WebSockets.

Quick start

The two smallest programs that join a room: one for the browser, one native. Both join the room lobby of the app webcpp-trystero-quick-start, so they meet each other, and any Trystero JS page that joins the same room, joinRoom({appId: 'webcpp-trystero-quick-start'}, 'lobby'), meets them both. Running the examples builds and runs them.

In the browser

A browser program keeps four things alive for as long as its page: an io_context, the browser::event_loop that drives it from the page’s JavaScript events, the browser::backend that implements the platform over the browser’s APIs, and the room. Actions are made from the room by name and payload type:

#include <webcpp/trystero.hpp>
#include <webcpp/trystero/browser/backend.hpp>
#include <webcpp/trystero/browser/src.hpp>  // once per program

#include <boost/asio/as_tuple.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/co_spawn.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/detached.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/use_awaitable.hpp>

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

namespace asio = boost::asio;
namespace trystero = webcpp::trystero;

/** What the page keeps alive: event loop, backend, room and actions. */
struct application {
    asio::io_context io;
    trystero::browser::event_loop loop{io};
    trystero::browser::backend backend{loop};
    trystero::room room{
        loop.get_executor(), backend, {.app_id = "webcpp-trystero-quick-start"}, "lobby"};
    trystero::action<std::string> chat = room.make_action<std::string>("chat");
    trystero::action<std::string> echo = room.make_action<std::string>("echo");
};

<webcpp/trystero/browser/src.hpp> is included in exactly one source file of the program: it defines the functions the page calls into the library with.

Handlers are set once the application exists. This program greets every peer that completes the handshake, prints every chat message, and starts a coroutine that answers the echo action:

int main() {
    auto* app = new application;  // a page's program lives as long as the tab

    app->room.on_peer_join([app](std::string_view peer) {
        trystero::send_options to_peer{.targets = {trystero::peer_id(peer)}, .metadata = {}};
        app->chat.async_send("hello", std::move(to_peer), [](boost::system::error_code ec) {
            if (ec) {
                std::cerr << "not delivered: " << ec.message() << '\n';
            }
        });
    });
    app->chat.on_message([](const std::string& text, const trystero::message_info& info) {
        std::cout << info.from << ": " << text << '\n';
    });
    asio::co_spawn(app->loop.get_executor(), echo_back(app->echo), asio::detached);
}

The coroutine awaits messages with async_receive and answers with async_send. boost::asio::as_tuple turns the error into a value, so leaving the room ends the loop instead of throwing:

/** Answers every message of the "echo" action, one at a time. */
asio::awaitable<void> echo_back(trystero::action<std::string>& echo) {
    for (;;) {
        auto [ec, text, info] = co_await echo.async_receive(asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
        if (ec) {
            co_return;  // the room was left
        }
        co_await echo.async_send("echo: " + text,
                                 trystero::send_options{.targets = {info.from}, .metadata = {}},
                                 asio::use_awaitable);
    }
}

main returns at once. Nothing blocks in a browser: every JavaScript event that reaches the library runs its handlers and then whatever became ready on the io_context (The browser backend).

Natively

The same room, natively, whole: a program that greets every peer that joins and prints what it receives on chat. A native program runs its io_context itself, since there is no event loop of a page to drive it, and the native backend posts what libdatachannel’s threads report to it:

#include <webcpp/trystero/native/backend.hpp>
#include <webcpp/trystero/room.hpp>

#include <boost/asio/io_context.hpp>

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

namespace trystero = webcpp::trystero;

int main() {
    boost::asio::io_context io;
    trystero::native::backend backend(io.get_executor());
    trystero::room room(io.get_executor(), backend, {.app_id = "webcpp-trystero-quick-start"},
                        "lobby");
    auto chat = room.make_action<std::string>("chat");

    room.on_peer_join([&](std::string_view peer) {
        trystero::send_options to_peer{.targets = {trystero::peer_id(peer)}, .metadata = {}};
        chat.async_send("hello from a native peer", std::move(to_peer),
                        [](boost::system::error_code) {});
    });
    chat.on_message([](const std::string& text, const trystero::message_info& info) {
        // flushed: into a pipe too, since the program runs until it is stopped
        std::cout << info.from << ": " << text << '\n' << std::flush;
    });

    io.run();  // lint-run: the program's network I/O; libdatachannel's threads post to it
}

io.run() returns only when the program is stopped: the room keeps its relays and its peers for as long as it lives.

Building

trystero is header-only, and is developed inside the webcpp superproject, as a Boost library is developed inside Boost. Besides Boost, it needs three libraries that are not part of it, which the build finds where b2’s command line says, else in the superproject’s .local/, until webcpp builds them from third_party/:

Library Needed by Found where

libsecp256k1 0.8.0, with its schnorrsig and extrakeys modules

every room: it signs the Nostr events peers meet through

-sSECP256K1_ROOT=<dir> natively, else .local/secp256k1-native; -sSECP256K1_EMSCRIPTEN_ROOT=<dir> for its emscripten build, else .local/secp256k1-emscripten

libdatachannel 0.24.6

the native backend

-sLIBDATACHANNEL_ROOT=<dir>, else .local/libdatachannel

OpenSSL 3

the native backend

-sOPENSSL_ROOT=<dir>, else .local/openssl

Each -s names a directory with the library’s include/ and lib/, on b2’s command line; the environment is never read, so that a variable a shell keeps from another day never replaces .local/ without a word. Without it, the library is looked for in the directory of .local/ that the table names, where webcpp’s continuous integration installs it, when that directory holds the library’s header, and else, natively outside Windows, in /usr/include or /usr/local/include, where a system install is legitimate. A relative -s is read from b2’s working directory. A -s that names a directory without the library’s header stops the build, naming it. A library found nowhere leaves trystero out: its tests and examples are skipped, the build says so once, naming the library and where it looked, and every other library builds; with webcpp-require-external=on, as the continuous integration builds, it stops the build instead. With MSVC, the libraries are CMake’s libsecp256k1.lib, which a program links statically with SECP256K1_STATIC defined, and OpenSSL’s libssl.lib and libcrypto.lib, also looked for in lib/VC/x64/MD, where the installer of Shining Light Productions puts them. trystero’s build.jam declares them so:

local secp256k1-root = [ webcpp.external trystero : libsecp256k1
    : SECP256K1_ROOT : secp256k1-native : secp256k1.h : native ] ;
local secp256k1-emscripten-root = [ webcpp.external trystero : libsecp256k1
    : SECP256K1_EMSCRIPTEN_ROOT : secp256k1-emscripten : secp256k1.h : emscripten ] ;
local libdatachannel-root = [ webcpp.external trystero : libdatachannel
    : LIBDATACHANNEL_ROOT : libdatachannel : rtc/rtc.hpp : native ] ;
local openssl-root = [ webcpp.external trystero : OpenSSL : OPENSSL_ROOT : openssl
    : openssl/ssl.h : native ] ;
lib secp256k1 : : <name>secp256k1 <toolset>emscripten
    <search>$(secp256k1-emscripten-root)/lib
  : : <include>$(secp256k1-emscripten-root)/include ;
lib secp256k1 : : <name>libsecp256k1 <toolset>msvc
    <search>$(secp256k1-root)/lib
  : : <include>$(secp256k1-root)/include <define>SECP256K1_STATIC ;
lib secp256k1 : : <name>secp256k1 <search>$(secp256k1-root)/lib
  : : <include>$(secp256k1-root)/include ;
lib datachannel : : <name>datachannel <search>$(libdatachannel-root)/lib
  : : <include>$(libdatachannel-root)/include
    <dll-path>$(libdatachannel-root)/lib ;
lib ssl : : <name>libssl <toolset>msvc <search>$(openssl-root)/lib
    <search>$(openssl-root)/lib/VC/x64/MD
  : : <include>$(openssl-root)/include ;
lib ssl : : <name>ssl <search>$(openssl-root)/lib
  : : <include>$(openssl-root)/include ;
lib crypto : : <name>libcrypto <toolset>msvc <search>$(openssl-root)/lib
    <search>$(openssl-root)/lib/VC/x64/MD
  : : <include>$(openssl-root)/include ;
lib crypto : : <name>crypto <search>$(openssl-root)/lib
  : : <include>$(openssl-root)/include ;

In a b2 project

A b2 project uses the rooms and the browser backend through /webcpp/trystero//trystero, which adds trystero’s headers, Boost’s, libsecp256k1 and Boost.JSON’s definitions, compiled once per variant, and, on emscripten, embind and BOOST_ASIO_DISABLE_THREADS, since the page has no threads:

alias trystero : : <conditional>@trystero-dependencies
  : : <include>include <library>/boost//headers <library>/webcpp//boost_json
  <library>/webcpp/config//config <library>secp256k1
  <toolset>emscripten:<define>BOOST_ASIO_DISABLE_THREADS
  <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-lembind ;

embind is linked as a flag, -lembind, rather than with b2’s own <embind>on: that feature is not free, and b2 ignores a feature that is not free among usage requirements, so a program that used it would not link.

A native program uses /webcpp/trystero//native, which adds libdatachannel and OpenSSL:

alias native : : <conditional>@native-dependencies
  : : <library>trystero <library>datachannel <library>ssl <library>crypto ;

The native backend’s WebRTC needs exceptions (Exceptions), and b2 lets no usage requirement override a build’s exception-handling=off, so each program and test that uses it declares <exception-handling>on itself, as the examples do:

webcpp.link native_quick_start : native_quick_start.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//native <exception-handling>on : native ;

and as trystero’s own tests of the native backend’s connections do:

webcpp.run native_peer_connection : native_peer_connection_test.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//native <exception-handling>on : native ;
webcpp.run native_room : native_room_test.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//native <exception-handling>on : native ;

A browser program is linked for the web, with a memory that grows:

webcpp.link quick_start : quick_start.cpp
  : <linkflags>-sENVIRONMENT=web <linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH : emscripten ;

The emscripten toolset

The emscripten target is b2’s emscripten toolset, registered against Emscripten 6.0.11 from emsdk, as a user-config.jam declares it, where $(emsdk) is the emsdk’s directory and $(node) the node that runs a program:

local emsdk = /path/to/emsdk ;
local node = /path/to/node ;
using emscripten : : $(emsdk)/upstream/emscripten/em++ : <nodejs>$(node) ;

With it and the three libraries found, from the root of a webcpp checkout, these build the tests and the examples, natively and on emscripten:

b2 libs/trystero/test libs/trystero/example
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/test libs/trystero/example

The three libraries

libsecp256k1 is built twice: natively, and with Emscripten for the browser. Its small tables keep the browser’s download small:

git clone --branch v0.8.0 https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1.git
options="-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF \
  -DSECP256K1_ENABLE_MODULE_SCHNORRSIG=ON -DSECP256K1_ENABLE_MODULE_EXTRAKEYS=ON \
  -DSECP256K1_ECMULT_WINDOW_SIZE=4 -DSECP256K1_ECMULT_GEN_KB=2 \
  -DSECP256K1_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DSECP256K1_BUILD_EXHAUSTIVE_TESTS=OFF \
  -DSECP256K1_BUILD_BENCHMARK=OFF"

cmake -S secp256k1 -B build-secp256k1-native $options \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PWD/webcpp/.local/secp256k1-native
cmake --build build-secp256k1-native && cmake --install build-secp256k1-native

emcmake cmake -S secp256k1 -B build-secp256k1-emscripten $options \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PWD/webcpp/.local/secp256k1-emscripten
cmake --build build-secp256k1-emscripten && cmake --install build-secp256k1-emscripten

where webcpp is the checkout of the superproject: each is installed in the directory of .local/ where the build looks for it.

libdatachannel is built with the compiler and the standard library that build the programs: a program built with GCC and libstdc++ does not link against a libdatachannel built with libc++, though the native headers still compile alone. Its own WebSocket is not used, so it is built without it, and its CMake finds OpenSSL where OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR says, which Homebrew’s OpenSSL needs, and which .local/openssl links for the build too:

openssl=$(brew --prefix openssl@3)  # or wherever OpenSSL 3 is
ln -s "$openssl" webcpp/.local/openssl

git clone --recurse-submodules --branch v0.24.6 \
  https://github.com/paullouisageneau/libdatachannel.git
cmake -S libdatachannel -B build-libdatachannel -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DNO_WEBSOCKET=ON -DNO_EXAMPLES=ON -DNO_TESTS=ON -DOPENSSL_ROOT_DIR=$openssl \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PWD/webcpp/.local/libdatachannel
cmake --build build-libdatachannel && cmake --install build-libdatachannel

Running the examples

The three examples need the public relays or a browser, so the build links them and never runs them: native_quick_start.cpp, natively; quick_start.cpp, a .js and a .wasm to embed in a page; and the chat, a page whose room is C++ (A page and its program). The quick starts meet in the room lobby of the app webcpp-trystero-quick-start, over the public relays; the chat joins the app and the room its user types, the room lobby of the app webcpp-trystero-chat unless the user changes them, and meets the quick starts when the user types theirs.

The native quick start is built as a program of its own, and runs until it is stopped:

b2 libs/trystero/example//native_quick_start-program
`find bin/libs/trystero/example -name native_quick_start-program -type f`

The chat is a page and its program, which the target site copies into a directory of its own under the build directory, out of the tree, and prints. The page is served from localhost, where crypto.subtle exists:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/example/chat//site
python3 -m http.server 8000 -d `find bin/libs/trystero/example/chat -name site -type d`

At http://localhost:8000, joining the app webcpp-trystero-quick-start, in place of the page’s webcpp-trystero-chat, and the room lobby brings the native quick start in as a peer within seconds: its greeting appears in the chat, and what the page sends is printed in its terminal. On another toolset, site stops the build, saying that the page is built on emscripten alone.

Rooms and actions

A room is what Trystero’s joinRoom returns, and an action what its makeAction returns: this section is the C++ form of both.

Joining

Constructing a room joins it: it connects to the relays and announces its peer on the room’s topic. It takes the executor every handler and completion of the room runs on, the backend, which must outlive it, its configuration, moved, and the room’s id. Its configuration, room_config, names the application, and everything else has Trystero’s default; the quick start builds one in place with designated initializers (In the browser):

Member What it is

app_id

The application’s id, Trystero’s appId: rooms of different apps never meet.

password

Trystero’s password: part of the key the signals are sealed with, and a challenge added to the handshake, so peers with another password never join. Empty, the signals are still sealed, under a key of the app and the room alone, and the handshake has no challenge.

relay_urls

The Nostr relays. Empty, the room uses relay_redundancy (5) of Trystero’s 29 default relays, chosen by a shuffle seeded with the app id, so that every peer of the app picks the same ones, as Trystero JS does.

ice_servers

The STUN and TURN servers; empty, Trystero’s STUN servers, default_ice_servers(). A server WebRTC would refuse, a URL that is not stun:, stuns:, turn: or turns: host[:port], or a TURN server without a user name and a credential, is dropped when the room joins and reported with error::invalid_configuration.

self_id

This peer’s id in the room, Trystero’s selfId; empty, 20 random characters, drawn for each room. One longer than 64 bytes, which other peers would ignore, is replaced and reported. Rooms of one app that meet a Trystero JS peer need ids of their own: Trystero keeps one connection per app and peer id, which all its rooms share, and drops a second one to the same id, while each room here makes its own, so two rooms given one id meet a Trystero JS peer in one of them only (Differences from Trystero).

handshake_timeout

How long a connected peer has to finish the handshake, 10 s.

max_receive_bytes

The most bytes the room reserves at once for the transfers it receives, across peers, 256 MiB.

log

Where the room’s diagnostics go, called with a category (nostr, signal, webrtc, room or action) and a sentence. Empty, no text is composed.

memory

The resource every allocation of the room goes through (Allocation).

room_config is move-only, since its log is a handler (Handlers): a room is given its configuration moved, or built in place.

Peers

on_peer_join and on_peer_leave set what is called with each peer whose handshake completed, and with each joined peer that leaves; peers() lists the joined peers. on_error sets what is called with each problem with one peer that the room handled itself, as Trystero’s onPeerError: a peer with another password, a handshake that timed out, a connection the backend refused. It is called with an empty peer id for each part of the configuration the room dropped when it joined, and for a count of signals that did not open with the room key (Bounded signaling). Each handler replaces the one set before, and every view it receives is valid for the call.

async_ping measures the round trip to a joined peer, from sending @_ping to receiving its @_pong.

async_leave says goodbye to every peer, Trystero’s @_leave, gives the farewell 99 ms, as Trystero waits, then closes the connections and the relay sockets, and every pending operation completes with error::room_left. Destroying a room leaves at once, without the 99 ms, and so does assigning another room over a joined one: every peer is told, and every pending operation completes with error::room_left, even while an action of it lives.

Actions

An action is a named channel of messages, wire compatible with Trystero’s makeAction. Its name has 1 to 32 UTF-8 bytes and no NUL; with another, every send fails with error::invalid_action_name. Its type says how messages travel and how they are received:

Type Trystero format Received as

std::string

text

a copy of the bytes

std::pmr::string

text

a copy of the bytes, in the room’s resource

std::string_view

text

a view of the frame it arrived in, valid during the handler

boost::json::value

JSON

parsed, in the room’s JSON storage

trystero::bytes

binary

a copy of the bytes

trystero::pmr_bytes

binary

the transfer’s buffer, moved, in the room’s resource

std::span<const std::uint8_t>

binary

a view of the frame, valid during the handler

trystero::payload

any

a std::variant of std::string, boost::json::value and bytes, by format

A message of another format than the action’s type is not delivered to it. Several actions of different types may share a name: one receives as views, another sends by moving strings, as the chat does (A page and its program).

Messages arrive at the handler on_message sets, with a message_info: the sender’s id and the metadata it passed. Without a handler they queue, up to 1024 per action, the oldest dropped first, for async_receive, which needs an owning type: a view would outlive the message. Frames of an action that arrived before it was made are kept, 64 per peer for 120 s, and delivered to it once it is.

async_send sends to send_options::targets, or to every joined peer, with optional JSON metadata. A payload that fits one 16 KiB frame with its header and metadata travels inline; a larger one is offered, accepted by the receiver within 120 s, and sent in chunks of at most 16,370 bytes. A frame or a chunk is handed to the data channel only while the channel buffers at most 64 KiB, waiting at most 10 s for it to drain. async_send completes once each target’s local data channel has taken the inline frame, or the last chunk of the transfer the receiver accepted, with the first failure if any, as Trystero’s send resolves: nothing confirms that the receiver has the message. A receiver takes one transfer per peer at a time, accepts it only for an action with a receiver, and reserves at most max_receive_bytes across peers.

Completion tokens and ownership

Every asynchronous operation is an Asio initiating function. With a callback it calls it on the room’s executor; with boost::asio::use_awaitable it resumes a coroutine; with boost::asio::deferred it returns an operation started later.

Because a deferred operation starts after the call, the arguments of an asynchronous operation are owned: async_send takes its value by value, moved when the type owns its storage, copied once at the call into the room’s resource when it is a view, and serialized at once when it is a boost::json::value; send_options owns its strings; and async_ping copies the peer id at the call. Everything else that only reads text takes a std::string_view.

Errors

Operations complete with a boost::system::error_code in the category webcpp.trystero, of the enumeration error:

Value Meaning

room_left

the room was left while the operation was pending

no_such_peer

the target is not a joined peer

peer_disconnected

the peer went away before the operation finished

invalid_action_name

an action’s name is not 1 to 32 UTF-8 bytes without NUL

metadata_too_large

the metadata does not fit one frame

transfer_rejected

the receiver refused the transfer, or a message had another format than the awaited type

transfer_timed_out

the receiver neither accepted nor refused within 120 s

channel_stalled

the data channel stopped draining for 10 s

wrong_password

a peer’s signals or handshake used another password, or a handshake message had the wrong shape

handshake_timed_out

a connected peer did not finish the handshake in time

handshake_failed

reserved: nothing reports it today

backend_failure

the browser or the native stack refused an operation

invalid_configuration

the configuration names something no backend can use; the room goes on without it

Allocation

A webcpp library lets its user choose where what it allocates comes from. trystero does it through std::pmr, header-only: every allocation of a room goes through one std::pmr::memory_resource, which its configuration names.

One resource per room

room_config::memory, which defaults to std::pmr::get_default_resource(), is the resource every allocation of the room goes through, from its construction to its destruction: the room itself, the copy of its configuration, its peers, actions, queues, frames, transfers, negotiations and relays, its handlers, the text it composes for its log, the objects its backend makes for it, the context libsecp256k1 signs with (secp256k1_context_preallocated_create, in the resource), and the JSON it parses and writes. A message an action’s handler receives as a std::pmr::string, a pmr_bytes or a boost::json::value is there too. trystero touches the resource only from the room’s executor, so it need not be thread-safe when that executor runs on one thread. A null memory is a programming error, which BOOST_ASSERT catches when the room is constructed.

trystero’s allocation test makes a configuration whose every part is in the resource it names: the strings and the relays’ URLs are made in it, and the log sink is a handler allocated there:

/** A room's configuration, every part of it in `memory`, made before the window. */
trystero::room_config config_in(counting_resource& memory, std::string_view self_id,
                                std::string_view relay, std::size_t& lines) {
    return trystero::room_config{
        .app_id = std::pmr::string("allocation", &memory),
        .password = std::pmr::string("a password", &memory),
        .relay_urls =
            std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>({std::pmr::string(relay, &memory)}, &memory),
        .self_id = std::pmr::string(self_id, &memory),
        .log =
            {
                std::allocator_arg,
                std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>(&memory),
                [&lines](std::string_view /*category*/, std::string_view /*text*/) { ++lines; },
            },
        .memory = &memory,
    };
}

How long the resource lives

The resource must outlive the room, every value the room handed out (a std::pmr::string, a pmr_bytes or a boost::json::value a handler kept), and every operation the room left pending: destroying a room closes everything, but what it closed still has operations queued that free into the resource. On Asio, the resource lives until the io_context of the room’s executor has run out of the room’s work or has been destroyed, so it is declared before the io_context, which is then destroyed first: the resource, then the io_context, then the room, in that order of declaration. In the browser, the resource lives until the room’s pending promises have settled, since a promise’s registration with the page’s event_loop keeps its handler, in the room’s resource; in practice, for the page’s life.

No check in debug builds catches the misuse: trystero holds a raw pointer and cannot see the resource end, and the use comes after the room is gone, from an operation of Asio’s or of the browser’s. A resource that asserts nothing is out when it is destroyed, as the test’s counting resources do, is the check, and it is the user’s.

A room allocates and frees on every event, a frame, a parsed text, a post or a log line, so a resource that reuses what is freed, a pool such as std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource, suits a long-lived room; a std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource grows with every event and suits a short-lived one, or a test.

Completion handlers

A completion handler is the user’s, and is allocated as its own associated allocator says: the room never binds its allocator over it. boost::asio::bind_allocator gives one the room’s resource. The allocation test makes the allocator of a resource:

const auto in = [](counting_resource& memory) {
    return std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>(&memory);
};

and binds it over the completions of a transfer and of a ping, so that they too are allocated in the sender’s resource:

a.make_action<trystero::pmr_bytes>("file").async_send(
    trystero::pmr_bytes(100'000, 7, &a_memory),
    boost::asio::bind_allocator(in(a_memory), [](boost::system::error_code /*ec*/) {}));
a.async_ping(z.self_id(),
             boost::asio::bind_allocator(
                 in(a_memory),
                 [&pings](boost::system::error_code ec,
                          std::chrono::milliseconds /*rtt*/) { pings += ec ? 0 : 1; }));

When the room erases a completion handler’s type (an any_completion_handler), it records whether the handler’s associated executor is the room’s, which only the concrete type tells without allocating; such a completion runs from an operation the room posts to its executor, allocated with the handler’s allocator. One bound to another executor is handed to that executor by Asio, whose type-erased executor wraps it with std::allocator.

Containers and shared objects

Every container trystero declares is a std::pmr one: std::pmr::string (and peer_id), std::pmr::vector (and backend::bytes, protocol::bytes and pmr_bytes), std::pmr::deque, std::pmr::map, std::pmr::set, std::pmr::unordered_map and std::pmr::unordered_set, built over the room’s resource; room_config, send_options, message_info and backend::ice_server hold them too. Two types stay the user’s choice of std::allocator: trystero::bytes, a std::vector<std::uint8_t>, and trystero::payload, a variant of std::string, boost::json::value and bytes. A received bytes, or the binary of a payload, is a copy of the frame, which is in the room’s resource.

A struct that holds std::pmr containers takes the room’s std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<> in its constructor, and a container of such structs is given it when it makes one, with try_emplace(key, allocator). A std::pmr container is never copied without an allocator: its copy constructor takes the default resource, so a copy names the resource, std::pmr::string(text, allocator). Moving keeps the resource.

Shared objects are made with std::allocate_shared over std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>, never with std::make_shared, std::make_unique or new; a timer is a std::shared_ptr for that reason.

Handlers

std::function takes no allocator since C++17, so trystero holds every handler it keeps in handler<R(Args...)>, a move-only callable that allocates through a std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>. Constructed with handler(std::allocator_arg, allocator, f), it holds f inline when f fits in three pointers and is nothrow-movable, and in storage of the allocator otherwise. It replaces every std::function of the backend interface (the handlers of its timer, WebSocket, data channel, peer connection and sealer), of the room and of the log’s sink. Constructed from f alone it uses the default resource; the room moves a handler it is given, room_config::log, into its own resource with the allocator-extended move. A move assignment carries the source’s allocator with its target.

Asio, the backends, Boost.JSON and the protocol

Asio. Every post, dispatch, timer wait and any_completion_handler the room makes carries boost::asio::bind_allocator over its resource. A post through boost::asio::any_io_executor is wrapped by Asio in a function object allocated with std::allocator, from Asio’s per-thread recycling cache, which calls std::aligned_alloc on a miss (measured: two per post, in every round of five posts, natively and on emscripten). So the room posts through the executor of an io_context when its executor is one, where Asio allocates the operation as the handler’s allocator says; on another executor, as the browser’s event_loop executor, the wrapper stays Asio’s.

The backends. Each method of backend::factory that makes an object takes the room’s std::pmr::memory_resource* as its last parameter, and the backend allocates its objects, their handlers and the frames and texts it hands to the room through it.

Boost.JSON allocates through json_resource, a boost::container::pmr::memory_resource that forwards to a std::pmr::memory_resource, header-only: the global resources of boost::container::pmr are compiled, and webcpp’s CI installs Boost’s headers alone. The room’s JSON storage is made once, when the room is constructed, since a value a handler keeps may outlive the room. Text is parsed by a boost::json::parser over that storage, never by boost::json::parse, whose temporaries beyond a stack buffer come from the default resource, and JSON is written by a boost::json::serializer whose stack is the resource.

The protocol (protocol/) takes a std::pmr::memory_resource* as the last parameter of every function that returns what it allocates, with the default resource as its default, and returns std::pmr types. protocol::nostr::verify uses secp256k1_context_static and allocates nothing.

What stays outside the resource

  • libdatachannel’s and OpenSSL’s own allocations, with the std::string and rtc::Description libdatachannel’s API takes and returns;

  • what emscripten::val holds, in the JavaScript heap;

  • the counter of the room’s JSON storage, which Boost.JSON allocates with operator new, once per room;

  • Asio’s own once-per-context allocations: its services and the scheduler’s first operation;

  • the wrapper Asio puts around a post through an executor that is not the executor of an io_context;

  • the native backend’s posts from libdatachannel’s threads, which carry Asio’s default allocator, since the resource is touched only on the room’s executor;

  • Boost.Beast’s and Asio’s state inside the native WebSocket: its stream, its resolver’s results, its coroutines’ frames;

  • the payload types std::string, bytes and payload, with std::allocator, the user’s choice;

  • on Emscripten, the C library’s select(), which Asio’s reactor calls on every wait of an io_context with a timer or a socket, and which callocs an array on every call.

The browser’s event_loop and the test’s memory relays are shared by every room of a page or of a test: they allocate the entries of their registrations and their relays through the resource they are constructed with, and a registered callback stays in its own resource, a room’s for a room’s object.

The proof

test/allocation_test.cpp, on both targets, counts the global operator new, which it replaces, and the C library’s allocation functions, where the platform lets a program see them: glibc’s are replaced and forward to __libc_*, Emscripten’s dlmalloc has weak definitions the test replaces, and macOS reports each to malloc_logger; MSVC’s are not counted, nor any under AddressSanitizer, whose own allocator reports to none of these. Only the thread main runs on is counted.

  • Two rooms over the memory relays exchange a payload, a std::pmr::string, a pmr_bytes and a boost::json::value in turn, while both counts see none and the counting resources of the two configurations see the rooms’.

  • Two rooms with a password, a log sink and the relays’ state in a resource of its own are made, join, exchange a payload that travels in chunks, measure a round trip, one says goodbye, both are destroyed and the io_context is drained. From the first construction to the drain, operator new sees exactly the two rooms’ JSON storage counters and the C library nothing. Once the rooms are destroyed their resources still have memory out, the operations they left pending, and none once the io_context has drained.

The counting resources also count a return of memory they never gave, a std::pmr object freed through the wrong resource, which must be none. Asio’s once-per-context allocations are made before anything is counted; without them the count is 8, not 2. On Emscripten the test also replaces select() with one that keeps its array on the stack, so that the count sees the rooms’ allocations rather than the C library’s wait. The test is declared in test/Jamfile:

webcpp.run allocation : allocation_test.cpp : <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH ;

The browser backend

In the browser, browser::backend implements the backend interface over the page’s own WebSocket, RTCPeerConnection, RTCDataChannel, setTimeout and crypto.subtle, through embind’s emscripten::val, and browser::event_loop runs the room’s executor from the page’s events. One of each serves every room of the page.

Driving Asio from the page’s event loop

In a browser nothing may block, and the page’s JavaScript event loop is the only source of events. An io_context never runs on its own there: browser::event_loop drives it without ever calling run().

  • Every JavaScript event that reaches the library, a socket’s message, a settled promise, an ICE candidate or a timer, is dispatched to its handler, and is followed by io_context::poll(), which runs everything that became ready.

  • Work given to the loop’s executor, browser::executor, while no JavaScript event is being handled posts to the io_context and schedules one poll() in a microtask.

  • The loop holds a work guard on the io_context, so a poll() never leaves it stopped.

So nothing runs while nothing happens, and a handler runs as soon as its event does. Two alternatives were rejected: poll() from emscripten_set_main_loop costs 60 wake-ups a second and stops in hidden tabs, where requestAnimationFrame does; poll() on a fixed interval costs wake-ups and up to an interval of latency. The backend’s timers are setTimeout, so their expiry is a JavaScript event like any other.

How JavaScript reaches C++

The page calls one function, trystero_dispatch, which <webcpp/trystero/browser/src.hpp> exports. A JavaScript handler is that function bound to the event loop, a registration and a slot. An object registers a callback with the loop and removes it when it is destroyed, so a late event for a destroyed object finds nothing; a destroyed loop marks every handler it made as dead.

Text that crosses into JavaScript is decoded straight from the WebAssembly memory a view points into, by a TextDecoder the loop keeps, and text that comes back is encoded by a TextEncoder straight into a string of the room’s resource: no std::string is made to carry either.

No JavaScript exception enters WebAssembly

The browser backend makes every call into JavaScript that can throw, a constructor, JSON.parse, a send, a WebRTC or Web Crypto method, through one function defined once in browser/src.hpp with EM_JS, which runs it inside try and returns a value or the exception as a value; the C++ turns that into the error its interface has. Every event of the page enters C++ through a function of the same file that catches what still escapes, puts WebAssembly’s stack pointer and the loop’s depth back as they were before the call, reports it and lets the loop poll again. With exceptions, browser::dispatch catches a C++ exception first, which frees it: one that reached JavaScript would keep its object for good. So a program that uses the browser backend may be built with exceptions or without them, and a peer’s malformed message never stops the page’s loop.

What a page bounds

  • A data channel message that is not an ArrayBuffer, as a text message a peer sends, or that is larger than any room frame (protocol::max_room_frame_bytes), is dropped before it is read: neither can be a frame.

  • A relay’s text longer than 1 MiB (protocol::max_relay_message_bytes) is not copied into WebAssembly: the socket closes, and reports the close.

  • A text that would take the socket’s bufferedAmount beyond 4 MiB (protocol::max_queued_relay_bytes), as when a relay stops reading, drops the socket, which reports one close at once. A page’s WebSocket cannot ping, so the browser has no idle timeout, which the native backend has (The relays).

  • A page makes at most browser::backend::max_peer_connections (256) peer connections, counted from their construction until the garbage collector frees them, as Chromium counts them against its own 500 (measured with headless Chrome: the 501st throws "Cannot create so many PeerConnections", and a closed one counts until a collection). Beyond, the rooms report each negotiation they cannot start, and the rest of Chromium’s count stays free for what the page makes without a room.

What a page needs

  • A secure context: https, or http on localhost or 127.0.0.1. Elsewhere crypto.subtle, which seals the signaling, does not exist, and every sealing operation fails with error::backend_failure.

  • No threads: Emscripten’s threads need a cross-origin isolated page, so trystero uses none. /webcpp/trystero//trystero defines BOOST_ASIO_DISABLE_THREADS on emscripten, and the loop drives Asio on the page’s one thread.

  • A program that lives as long as the page: the event loop must outlive every room and object it serves.

  • Boost.JSON’s definitions, which a program links from /webcpp//boost_json, which /webcpp/trystero//trystero brings and which builds on emscripten as on every target.

A page and its program

The chat example is a page whose room is C++: the program joins and sends, and the page only draws. It keeps the loop, the backend and the room for the page’s life, and makes the action chat twice: once as std::string_view, to receive a message as a view of its frame, and once as std::string, to send by moving the text:

struct chat {
    boost::asio::io_context io;
    trystero::browser::event_loop loop{io};
    trystero::browser::backend backend{loop};
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::room> room;
    // The action "chat" twice: received as views of the frame, and sent by moving the text.
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::action<std::string_view>> messages;
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::action<std::string>> outgoing;
};

The page calls join with the app and the room its user typed, and the program joins and sets its handlers; a received message goes from its frame straight into a JavaScript string:

void join_room(const std::string& app_id, const std::string& room_id) {
    auto& c = the_chat();
    if (c.room) {
        return;
    }
    trystero::room_config config;
    config.app_id = app_id;
    config.log = [](std::string_view category, std::string_view text) {
        ui("log", category, text);
    };
    c.room = std::make_unique<trystero::room>(c.loop.get_executor(), c.backend, std::move(config),
                                              room_id);
    c.messages = std::make_unique<trystero::action<std::string_view>>(
        c.room->make_action<std::string_view>("chat"));
    c.outgoing =
        std::make_unique<trystero::action<std::string>>(c.room->make_action<std::string>("chat"));
    c.room->on_peer_join([](std::string_view peer) { ui("peerJoined", peer); });
    c.room->on_peer_leave([](std::string_view peer) { ui("peerLeft", peer); });
    // A view of the received frame: the text goes from the frame straight into a JavaScript string.
    c.messages->on_message([](std::string_view text, const trystero::message_info& info) {
        ui("message", std::string_view(info.from), text, false);
    });
    ui("joined", c.room->self_id(), std::string_view(room_id));
}

send shows the message at once, and reports a failure in the page’s log:

void send_message(std::string text) {
    auto& c = the_chat();
    if (!c.room || text.empty()) {
        return;
    }
    ui("message", c.room->self_id(), std::string_view(text), true);
    c.outgoing->async_send(std::move(text), [](boost::system::error_code ec) {
        if (ec) {
            ui("log", std::string_view("chat"), std::string_view("not delivered: " + ec.message()));
        }
    });
}

The two functions are what the program exports to the page, through embind:

EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS(chat_example) {
    emscripten::function("join", &join_room);
    emscripten::function("send", &send_message);
}

Any Trystero JS page, or any other page of the chat, that joins the same app and room is in the same chat (Running the examples).

The native backend

Natively, native::backend implements the backend interface over libdatachannel for WebRTC, Boost.Beast for the relays’ WebSockets, OpenSSL for TLS and AES-GCM, and Asio’s timers. A native room is the same room as a browser’s or Trystero JS’s: they meet over the same relays and exchange the same frames. One backend serves every room of the application, beside the executor it runs on, and a native program runs that executor’s io_context itself, blocking on it or polling it (Natively).

Exceptions

trystero raises no exception of its own, but libdatachannel reports errors by throwing, and the native backend’s data channel and peer connection catch what it throws on refused input and complete with error::backend_failure. So they need exceptions: without them, or with WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS or WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_NO_EXCEPTIONS defined, native::data_channel, native::peer_connection and native::backend, which makes their objects, do not exist, and code that uses them does not compile. The native timer, sealer and WebSockets, and the rest of trystero, are unchanged.

<webcpp/trystero/config.hpp>, which every header includes first, defines WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_NO_EXCEPTIONS when webcpp has no exceptions (WEBCPP_HAS_EXCEPTIONS is not defined: the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS); a developer may define it for trystero alone in a build that has them. Each program and test that uses the native backend’s WebRTC declares <exception-handling>on itself, whatever the build asks (In a b2 project). One function of the backend throws: its constructor, a boost::system::system_error when OpenSSL cannot make the TLS context or load the system’s certificate authorities.

Threads

libdatachannel delivers its events on threads of its own. The backend never runs a handler there: each event copies what it carries and is posted to the room’s executor, through a weak reference, so an event that arrives after its object is gone does nothing. Every handler of the room and every completion runs on the executor, as in the browser. An application that runs the io_context on several threads gives the room a strand.

A received data channel message is copied once, out of libdatachannel’s std::vector<std::byte> into the room’s resource, on the executor; from there it is delivered without another copy. A text message, as a peer can send, or a binary one larger than any room frame, is dropped on libdatachannel’s thread: neither can be a frame.

What the backend asks of libdatachannel

  • Automatic negotiation is off, so an offer or an answer exists only when the signaling asks for one, as in the browser.

  • Every object libdatachannel hands out is held by the backend: libdatachannel keeps only weak references.

  • Local candidates leave as the JSON of an RTCIceCandidateInit, the form Trystero JS adds with addIceCandidate.

  • The rtc::PeerConnection object and its control block are made in the room’s resource; what that object allocates inside libdatachannel is libdatachannel’s (What stays outside the resource).

Its configuration

native::backend_config is what the backend makes its peer connections with, beside the room’s ice_servers:

Member What it is

bind_address

The local address every peer connection binds to, as "127.0.0.1"; empty means every interface but the loopback. Bound to the loopback, the peers of one machine connect with no other network, which a test wants; a peer bound there reaches no other machine.

max_peer_connections_per_minute

The most peer connections the backend makes in any minute, for every room it serves together, 256: beyond, it makes none, and a room reports each negotiation it cannot start. A room makes at most 64 in any 57 s however its peers behave (Bounded signaling), so the default lets four rooms do so at once.

relay_limits

What the relays’ WebSockets tolerate of a relay that stops reading or answering, native::websocket_limits (The relays).

The relays

The relays are reached over Boost.Beast: ws:// in the clear, wss:// over TLS with SNI and host name verification. The backend verifies relays against the system’s certificate authorities; tls_context() gives the boost::asio::ssl::context to an application with authorities of its own. A relay whose certificate does not verify is unreachable, and the room retries it later as it would any other. The WebSockets are Beast’s rather than libdatachannel’s own, so the relays run on the room’s executor like everything else.

A relay is a third party, and the backend bounds what one can make the room hold:

  • A text longer than 1 MiB (protocol::max_relay_message_bytes) closes the connection before it is copied, as in the browser.

  • A relay that stops reading is dropped once the text held unsent for it would pass 4 MiB (websocket_limits::max_queued_bytes, which is protocol::max_queued_relay_bytes on both backends).

  • A relay that stops answering is dropped once idle_timeout (30 s) passes with its keep-alive ping unanswered: halfway through, the connection sends a ping. The timeout counts bytes received, and a ping waits for the write in flight, so a relay that reads under about 2 KB/s is closed during a 64 KiB text. Signaling texts are 2 to 4 KB, so a real room meets it only with a relay slower than about 200 B/s.

Each drop reports one close, and the room reconnects with its backoff (Discovery over Nostr). A page has no idle timeout: its WebSocket cannot ping (What a page bounds).

The protocol

A room keeps Trystero 0.26.0’s wire byte for byte. The protocol’s pure functions are in <webcpp/trystero/protocol/>; their tests compare them, byte for byte, with values Trystero JS computed itself (Testing). What a Trystero JS peer or a page sees never changes: the topic prefixes Trystero@ and Trystero:, the handshake’s __trystero_pw, every constant and message layout, and the default relays in their order.

Discovery over Nostr

Part What it is

Root topic

Trystero’s sha1 of Trystero@<app>@<room>: each SHA-1 byte in base 36, unpadded, concatenated

Peer topic

the same of Trystero@<app>@<room>@<peer id>, where a peer receives its offers, answers and candidates

Event

kind 20000 plus the sum of the topic’s UTF-16 code units modulo 10000, ephemeral; the topic in an x tag; signed with BIP-340

Subscription

one per relay, to the root topic and the peer’s own topic

Announcement

{"peerId":...,"nonce":...} on the root topic: at once, then after 233, 533, 1333 and 5333 ms, then every 60 s

Relays

the configured ones, or 5 of Trystero’s 29 defaults, shuffled with sin(seed++) * 10000 seeded by the app id

A relay that answers rate-limited: is skipped for 60 s, doubling to 15 minutes while the replies persist; one that answers blocked:, restricted:, auth-required: or pow: is retired. A lost relay is reconnected after a random share of 3.3 s, doubling to 60 s, and the delay comes back to 3.3 s only once a connection stayed open for 60 s, so that a relay that closes the room at once after each open is tried less and less often.

Signaling

Of two peers, the one with the lower id offers, on the relay that carried the other’s announcement. The higher one answers an announcement by announcing itself on the other’s peer topic, so the lower one offers: at most once a second per peer, and once in 5.3 s per relay for the whole room, Trystero’s announce interval, so that a flood of low ids does not have the relays rate-limit the room. Offers, answers and candidates are sealed with AES-GCM under the SHA-256 of <password>:<app>:<room>, the password empty when there is none, with a 16-byte IV, as the text <iv>$<ciphertext>: the IV’s bytes in decimal joined by commas, and the ciphertext with its tag in base64. Candidates follow their offer or answer, trickled. A negotiation ends when the data channel opens: the connection is the room’s, and signals from that peer are ignored until it leaves.

The data channel

Every message is a room frame: 1, the length of the room token (16 bits, big-endian), the token, the hexadecimal SHA-256 of Trystero:<app>:<room>, then an action frame. A presence frame, 2, present or not, the token’s length and the token, announces or withdraws the room.

Action frames are Trystero’s action wire, version 2: an inline frame carries the payload whole; a larger payload is an offer, accepted or refused by the receiver, then chunks of at most 16,370 bytes, in order. Integers and float64 values are big-endian, as JavaScript’s DataView writes them.

Frame Bytes

inline (kind 0)

2, the kind and the format shifted by four, the name (32 bytes, NUL padded), the metadata’s length (uint16), the metadata, the payload

offer (kind 1)

the inline header, the transfer’s id (uint32), the payload’s size (float64), the metadata

chunk (kind 2)

2, 2, the transfer’s id (uint32), the offset (float64), the bytes

accepted (kind 3)

2, 3, the transfer’s id (uint32)

rejected (kind 4)

2, 4, the transfer’s id (uint32), the reason (UTF-8, at most 200 bytes)

cancelled (kind 5)

2, 5, the transfer’s id (uint32)

The payload’s format is text (0), JSON (1) or binary (2). Internal actions run the room:

Action What it carries

@_hsdata

the password handshake: the lower id sends a challenge, and the other answers with the hexadecimal SHA-256 of <challenge>:<password>:<app>:<room>

@_hsready

the sender’s side of the handshake passed; a peer joins when both sides sent it

@_ping, @_pong

round trips

@_leave

the sender leaves the room

The media actions, @_stream, @_track and @_signal, are not ported (Differences from Trystero): a frame of one is ignored.

Bounded signaling

Announcements are not sealed, so anyone who knows the app and room ids can announce any number of peer ids, and anyone who reads the relays can send any signal in any peer’s name. Trystero JS bounds none of this; trystero bounds what each costs a room.

  • Nothing a peer sends changes a negotiation before it opens with the room key: an offer, an answer or a candidate that does not open is counted, reported once per negotiation, and changes nothing else. A flood of fresh ids makes each a negotiation, so the reports are paced: the first of a quiet 10 s goes to on_error at once, with its peer, and the others of those 10 s in one report, with no peer and their number.

  • A room holds at most detail::signaling::max_unconnected_peers (32) negotiations with peers it is not connected to. A negotiation whose offer and answer expire without a connection is dropped, an idle one gives its place to a new peer, and a new peer beyond the bound is refused and logged once.

  • A room makes at most max_connections_per_window (64) connections in any 57 s, however soon they end, and a page at most 256 (What a page bounds); the native backend makes at most 256 a minute (Its configuration).

  • A signal’s fields are bounded in protocol/signal.hpp: the peer id (64 bytes; Trystero’s are 20), the offer id (64 bytes), a sealed offer or answer (64 KiB) and a sealed candidate (16 KiB, above the 8192 bytes of plaintext Trystero takes).

  • A relay is a third party too: its texts are bounded at 1 MiB, what the room holds unsent for it at 4 MiB, and, natively, its silence at 30 s (The relays).

Replayed offers and answers

A sealed offer or answer holds neither its offer id nor a peer id (Trystero’s wire), so one recorded from the relays still opens when anyone resends it in its sender’s name, and so does the room’s own, sent back to it. A room remembers, by the SHA-256 of their opened text, the last 1024 offers and answers it made or acted on (detail::signaling::remembered_descriptions), and refuses one that comes to it as a peer’s: it changes nothing and is logged. It makes or acts on at most two per connection it makes, so each is remembered for at least an offer’s lifetime (57 s), and in a quiet room for its whole life. So a room refuses a sealed offer or answer it acted on, resent, and one it made itself, sent back as a peer’s offer or answer.

What remains

Two limitations remain, both of Trystero’s wire, which only a change that Trystero JS shares can close.

A watcher without the key can keep two peers apart. A sealed offer or answer the room neither made nor acted on still opens and is acted on. Such texts are not scarce: every peer seals a fresh offer for any id announced above its own, and announcements need no key. So anyone who reads and publishes on the relays, without the key, can keep any two peers of a room apart from their first meeting for as long as it keeps at it, each attempt costing the other peer a connection of its window. It cannot read or alter anything the peers exchange, join the room, or touch peers already joined; a joined peer that drops is a new peer again. The room refuses only what it made or already acted on. Only a wire that seals the offer id and both peer ids closes this, which Trystero would have to share (reported upstream).

A flooder can delay new peers. Joined peers, memory and connections stay safe under a flood, but a flooder who keeps sending new ids takes each place, or each connection of the window, as it frees, so new peers can be kept out for as long as the flood lasts, each place up to one offer’s lifetime (57 s) at a time. A joined peer whose connection drops comes back as a new peer, with the same id, and is kept out the same way: the room has no renegotiation that would keep its place. Closing it needs announcements that prove the room key, a wire change Trystero would have to share.

Design

Layers

Layer Headers Knows

Protocol

protocol/*.hpp

pure functions over bytes and text: no I/O, no platform

Backend interface

backend.hpp

the WebSocket, peer connection, data channel, timer and AES-GCM sealer a platform provides

Room

room.hpp, detail/*.hpp

the Nostr strategy, the signaling, the peer links, the action wire and the public API

Browser backend

browser/*.hpp

emscripten::val over the browser’s APIs, and the event loop

Native backend

native/*.hpp

libdatachannel, Boost.Beast, OpenSSL and Asio’s timers

Everything above the backend interface is the core, which builds on both targets: the same room runs over the browser’s APIs, over libdatachannel, and over the memory relays of the tests (Testing). The core never includes a backend, libdatachannel, OpenSSL or Emscripten: a boundary of the library’s own, which webcpp’s lint checks, keeps it so.

Why abstract classes for the backend

The backend is a handful of abstract classes rather than template parameters. Each of its operations is a call into JavaScript or into a network stack, so a virtual call costs nothing measurable, while the room’s code stays free of templates over the platform and of #ifdef, and the test backend and the browser backend are interchangeable at run time. Every handler a backend invokes runs on the room’s executor, after the call that caused it has returned, never inside it: the room calls these operations from inside handlers whose state a completion run there would change under them.

Why the browser’s own WebRTC

libdatachannel’s WebAssembly port, datachannel-wasm, has no media and hides the RTCPeerConnection it wraps. Binding the browser’s objects directly through emscripten::val is smaller than that wrapper, reports every error, and leaves the browser’s whole WebRTC stack (capture, codecs, playout) within reach for media.

Text is a view, a copy is a decision

A parameter that only reads text is a std::string_view, bytes are a std::span, and a string is used where something must own the text: a map key, a member, a capture of a handler that runs later.

  • The digests the protocol takes are fed the parts of their input: nothing is concatenated to hash it.

  • Signals and relay messages are read as views into the parsed document; the JSON the room writes goes into one reserved buffer, escaped by Boost.JSON’s serializer, and a Nostr event’s id is hashed over those same bytes.

  • A frame is written once, inside its room envelope, and shared by every target; a received frame becomes the buffer of the message delivered from it, and a view handler reads it in place.

  • A sentence of the log is composed only when there is a sink.

The asynchronous operations are the exception, for the reason Completion tokens and ownership gives.

Optional native dependencies

libdatachannel is under the MPL 2.0 and OpenSSL under the Apache License 2.0. Both are needed only by the native backend, which a browser program never includes: /webcpp/trystero//trystero depends on neither, and /webcpp/trystero//native adds them, as OpenSSL is optional for Asio.

Licensing

The library is distributed under the Boost Software License. It ports Trystero’s protocol and was written with Trystero’s source open, so Trystero’s MIT notice comes with it (Acknowledgements).

Guarantees

What trystero promises, and the test that holds each promise, which fails when the promise breaks. A guarantee keeps its number, and the anchor named after it, so a comment of the code or of a test cites it by that anchor: (doc: #trystero-invariant-3) sends its reader to the third. b2 libs/trystero/doc, which builds this page, fails on a citation that names no anchor of it. The tests are those of Testing.

  1. The wire is Trystero 0.26.0’s. A C++ peer, in the browser or native, and Trystero JS peers in one room join, exchange text, JSON and binary messages, files both ways with metadata, and pings, leave, and form a mesh, with either side offering. Held by the interop lane, interop_browser on emscripten and interop_native natively, against Trystero 0.26.0 itself in headless Chrome.

  2. Every protocol value equals Trystero JS’s. Topics, room tokens, the relay shuffle, sealed text, Nostr event ids, inline and chunked action frames, control frames, envelopes and presence are what Trystero’s own functions compute from the same inputs, byte for byte. Held by protocol, against the values the oracle lane has Trystero 0.26.0 write, and by the oracle lane, which fails when Trystero would write other values than those committed; and by native_sealer, which opens what Trystero JS sealed with Web Crypto.

  3. A peer with another password never joins. Its signals do not open, and its handshake fails, so neither side reports it joined. Held by room (the_same_password_joins_and_another_does_not), native_room (another_password_never_joins), and the wrong-password scenario of the interop lane.

  4. A payload larger than a frame travels in chunks, both ways. It is offered, accepted and sent in chunks of at most 16,370 bytes, and arrives whole, from either peer. Held by room (large_payloads_travel_in_chunks_both_ways, 100 KB each way), and the file transfers of the interop lane.

  5. Every allocation of a room goes through its resource, but what What stays outside the resource lists: from its construction until its io_context has drained, the global operator new sees only the room’s JSON storage counter, and the C library nothing. Held by allocation, natively and on emscripten.

  6. No unit test reaches beyond the loopback. The rooms of the unit tests meet over the memory relays, the native tests’ peer connections bind to 127.0.0.1 and gather their candidates there alone, and the WebSocket test talks to a server of its own on 127.0.0.1. Held by the container lanes, gcc-14 and clang-linux-18: every unit test, built with GCC 14 and with clang 18 against libstdc++, passes in a Linux container that has no network but the loopback (docker run with the network none).

  7. A room refuses a replayed or reflected offer or answer. A sealed offer or answer it made, or acted on, that comes back to it as a peer’s changes nothing (Replayed offers and answers). Held by room (a_replayed_answer_is_refused, a_replayed_offer_is_refused, a_reflected_offer_is_refused_as_an_answer, a_reflected_offer_is_refused_as_an_offer and a_reflected_answer_is_refused_as_an_answer), and the replay and reflection scenarios of the interop lane.

  8. A relay that stops reading is dropped. Once the text held unsent for it would pass 4 MiB, the connection is dropped, and reports one close, after which the room reconnects with its backoff, as it does to any relay that closes. Held by native_websocket (a_relay_that_stops_reading_is_dropped_at_the_queue_bound, a close before 2000 texts of 64 KiB, and one only) natively, and browser_websocket_bound on emscripten, with exceptions and without them, which also checks that the socket never holds more than 4 MiB; the reconnection by room (a_relay_that_closes_at_once_is_tried_less_and_less_often).

Testing

Testing a program that uses trystero

A room needs relays and peers, and a test needs neither the network nor another machine. The backend interface is the seam: a program’s tests run its rooms over a backend of their own, in memory, as trystero’s own tests run whole rooms over test/support/memory_backend.hpp, a backend whose Nostr relays forward ephemeral events to matching subscriptions, whose peer connections pair through their descriptions, whose data channels deliver in order, and whose sealer opens only what was sealed under the same key, each event posted to the io_context. It is in the namespace webcpp::trystero::test, outside the library’s public headers, and a program may copy it.

A test of the native backend’s own WebRTC binds its connections to the loopback, native::backend_config::bind_address set to "127.0.0.1", and names a STUN server where nothing answers, stun:127.0.0.1:9, in place of Trystero’s public ones: the loopback’s host candidate is then the only one, and it is enough.

How trystero is tested

trystero’s tests are under test/, each declared in test/Jamfile, and each guarantee of Guarantees names the tests that hold it. They run on two targets: 63 tests in all, 42 natively and 51 on emscripten, under node. The protocol, the rooms and the allocation test run on both:

webcpp.run protocol : protocol_test.cpp : <testing.input-file>fixtures/expected/expected.json ;
webcpp.run room : room_test.cpp ;
webcpp.run allocation : allocation_test.cpp : <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH ;
Test What it checks

the public headers

Each compiled alone, on each target that builds it: the core on both, the native backend natively, against libdatachannel and OpenSSL, and the browser backend on emscripten.

config, config_developer_defined, config_all_off

<webcpp/trystero/config.hpp> defines WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_NO_EXCEPTIONS exactly when webcpp has no exceptions (WEBCPP_HAS_EXCEPTIONS is not defined: the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS), and keeps it when a developer defines it for trystero alone in a build that has them.

protocol

The protocol against values Trystero JS 0.26.0 computed itself: topics, room tokens, the relay shuffle, sealed text, Nostr event ids, inline and chunked action frames, control frames, envelopes and presence, and the bounds of a signal’s fields.

room

Whole rooms in one process, over the memory relays: every payload format, 100 KB transfers both ways, ping, passwords right and wrong, leaving and returning, a room moved over a joined one, ICE servers checked as WebRTC checks them, floods of announcements and of forged, replayed and reflected signals, a relay that closes at once or rate-limits, a three-peer mesh, coroutines and view handlers.

allocation

Every allocation of two rooms goes through their resources (The proof).

native_sealer, native_websocket, native_timer

The native backend, part by part, natively: the sealer opens what Trystero JS sealed with Web Crypto; the WebSocket, against a Beast server in the same process, opens, sends in order, closes once, and drops a relay that sends too much, stops reading or stops answering, while one that answers its pings stays; the timer never fires once cancelled, restarted or destroyed.

native_peer_connection, native_room

Two libdatachannel connections wired to each other, each handler on the executor, and whole native rooms over real libdatachannel connections, bound to 127.0.0.1.

browser_event_loop, browser_websocket, browser_websocket_bound, browser_websocket_late_events, browser_sealer, browser_data_channel, browser_peer_connection

The browser backend, on emscripten under node, which has the page’s WebSocket, Web Crypto and microtasks but no WebRTC: the loop and its recovery from exceptions that escape a callback, the WebSocket’s URLs, its bound on what a relay holds unsent and its silence once dropped, the sealer’s completions, a data channel’s refusal of what is no frame, and the page’s peer connections, made or refused, and their census.

The native backend’s connections need exceptions whatever the build asks (Exceptions), and each browser test is also built without exceptions, as a program that uses the browser backend may be:

webcpp.run browser_event_loop : browser_event_loop_test.cpp : : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_websocket : browser_websocket_test.cpp : : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_websocket_bound : browser_websocket_bound_test.cpp : : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_websocket_late_events : browser_websocket_late_events_test.cpp : : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_sealer : browser_sealer_test.cpp : : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_data_channel : browser_data_channel_test.cpp : : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_peer_connection : browser_peer_connection_test.cpp : : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_event_loop_no_exceptions : browser_event_loop_test.cpp
  : <exception-handling>off : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_websocket_no_exceptions : browser_websocket_test.cpp
  : <exception-handling>off : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_websocket_bound_no_exceptions : browser_websocket_bound_test.cpp
  : <exception-handling>off : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_websocket_late_events_no_exceptions : browser_websocket_late_events_test.cpp
  : <exception-handling>off : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_sealer_no_exceptions : browser_sealer_test.cpp
  : <exception-handling>off : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_data_channel_no_exceptions : browser_data_channel_test.cpp
  : <exception-handling>off : emscripten ;
webcpp.run browser_peer_connection_no_exceptions : browser_peer_connection_test.cpp
  : <exception-handling>off : emscripten ;

From the root of a webcpp checkout, with the three libraries of Building found, each of these builds and runs the tests, natively, under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and on emscripten:

b2 libs/trystero/test
b2 libs/trystero/test address-sanitizer=norecover undefined-sanitizer=norecover
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/test

The 3 examples are linked and never run, since each needs the public relays or a browser. b2 compares timestamps, so a result that counts is built from scratch, with b2 -a.

The oracle and the interop lanes

Two lanes of trystero’s own, declared in test/oracle/Jamfile, check it against Trystero itself, pinned at 0.26.0 by test/oracle/package.json and package-lock.json, with Node:

webcpp.original node ;
webcpp.cases protocol : oracle.mjs : ../fixtures/cases : ../fixtures/expected ;
webcpp.lane oracle : cases-protocol ;

oracle, which names no target, runs Trystero’s own functions over the inputs of test/fixtures/cases/protocol.json and checks that they still write test/fixtures/expected/expected.json byte for byte, the values the protocol and native_sealer tests reproduce; update-expected is its only writer.

webcpp.drive interop_browser : interop/peer.cpp
  : <linkflags>-sENVIRONMENT=web <linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH <webcpp-drive-timeout>900
  : interop/run.mjs : --browser : emscripten ;
webcpp.drive interop_native : interop/native_peer.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//native <exception-handling>on <webcpp-drive-timeout>900
    <define>_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_EXTENSIVE
    <define>_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
  : interop/run.mjs : --native : native ;
webcpp.lane interop : interop_browser interop_native : native emscripten ;

interop, natively and on emscripten, meets each C++ peer, the native one as a process and the browser’s in headless Chrome, with Trystero JS peers in Chrome, over an in-memory Nostr relay on 127.0.0.1 that verifies every event’s id and signature as a public relay does. Its scenarios: the C++ peer offering; Trystero JS offering, with a password; a Trystero JS peer that also sends malformed candidates, or text messages on its data channel; a first relay to which no WebSocket can be made; a C++ peer given a TURN server without credentials; a watcher without the key that answers every offer with garbage in the other peer’s name, that resends a sealed answer and offer it recorded, and that sends the C++ peer its own sealed offer back, which the C++ peer must refuse; a flood of announcements and of unsealed offers from fresh peer ids; a relay text longer than 1 MiB; a C++ peer and a Trystero JS page each in two rooms of one app, every C++ room with its own peer id (Where a ported feature behaves otherwise); a wrong password; and a mesh of three. The native peer meets three more: a room moved over the joined one, which must leave it as destroying it does; a relay that ends the connection just as the peer writes, which twelve peers in turn must survive; and the driver’s own check that a peer killed by a signal is named at once.

Every peer gathers its ICE candidates on the machine alone: the C++ peers get stun:127.0.0.1:9 in place of Trystero’s public STUN servers, the native peer binds its connections to 127.0.0.1, and the Trystero JS peers have no ICE server. Chrome is the one CHROME names, else on macOS Playwright’s chrome-headless-shell; the continuous integration names Chrome for Testing’s chrome-headless-shell, at the version webcpp pins. Each driver is bounded by 900 s, beyond its scenarios’ own limits, so that a scenario that does not complete fails by name with what each peer saw.

b2 -a libs/trystero/test/oracle//oracle
b2 -a --dump-tests --out-xml=native.trystero.interop.xml libs/trystero/test/oracle//interop
b2 -a --dump-tests --out-xml=emscripten.trystero.interop.xml toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/test/oracle//interop

The container lanes

Two lanes of the continuous integration, gcc-14 and clang-linux-18, build and run the unit tests with GCC 14 and with clang 18 against libstdc++ in a Linux container, Ubuntu 24.04, with docker run and the network none, which leaves the loopback alone: every test passes, which shows that none reaches beyond the machine (guarantee 6). libsecp256k1 and libdatachannel are built before, on the runner, Ubuntu 24.04 too, with the lane’s compiler against the runner’s OpenSSL 3, and the container, which holds the same compilers and OpenSSL’s development files, sees them where the runner put them.

The test matrix

The continuous integration runs trystero’s tests in lanes, one toolset each, and its own lanes, the oracle once and the interop natively and on emscripten, as native.trystero.interop and emscripten.trystero.interop. Each lane builds from scratch and records what b2 built and ran; webcpp’s tools/report/report.py merges the files of every lane into a matrix, where each cell says whether that program passed in that lane, or how it failed. The matrix is published with the documentation, at https://webcpporg.github.io/report/.

Reference

Every name trystero declares, in the namespace webcpp::trystero and those nested in it, from the Doc Comments of its headers: each class, function, type and enumerator with its declaration, what it does, what it asks of its caller and how it fails, and the part of Trystero 0.26.0 it ports. The other sections teach the library; this one is where a name is looked up.

webcpp::trystero::backend

The seam between the room and a platform: what a target must provide for a room to run on it. The browser provides it over emscripten::val (webcpp/trystero/browser), a native target over libdatachannel, Boost.Beast and OpenSSL (webcpp/trystero/native), and the tests over memory (test/support).

Description

Tip: every handler a backend invokes runs on the room’s executor, one at a time, and may destroy the object that invoked it. A backend whose events arrive on other threads (libdatachannel) posts them there first.

Every handler runs after the call that caused it has returned, never inside it: a completion (done) of a peer_connection or a sealer, and a websocket’s close when no socket can be made, are posted even when their result is known at once. The room calls these operations from inside handlers whose state a completion run there would change under them.

Text crosses this interface as std::string_view, valid for the duration of the call or of the handler: a backend reads what it is given before returning, and a handler copies what it keeps. The one exception is a data channel message, handed over by value: the receiver keeps the frame, and taking ownership of it is what spares a copy.

Tip: every method that makes an object takes the room’s memory resource last, and the backend allocates the object, its handlers and what it hands to the room (a frame, a text) through it, on the room’s executor only.
